title: Kyoto in 2 Days: Sake, Sweets, and a Soak
description: Spend two days in Kyoto wandering Fushimi’s shrine and sake lanes, exploring Nishijin’s weaving streets, tasting a seasonal sweet, and soaking at Funaoka Onsen.
published: 2026-11-25
updated: 2026-11-25
illustration: 81e037f36011788235c27c92033453cdbc0d3cd6e0ea84a7478e4c4fd5b581ea
illustrationAlt: Painted illustration of a 2-day trip in Kyoto
---
Sake, Sweets, and a Soak is a two-day Kyoto trip for a first-time visitor who wants to explore local culture, enjoy a traditional sweet, and finish with a bathhouse soak.

The plan moves from Fushimi’s shrine and sake lanes to Nishijin’s weaving district and a bath in Kita. Each stop has a suggested time and duration, so you can follow the day at an easy pace.

## Day 1: Fushimi’s Shrine and Sake Lanes

![Painted illustration for day 1 in Kyoto: Fushimi’s shrine and sake lanes](/media/trip-story/c29ccf3b0204f55dd2592f1aa988d9de695df4edc63ff136d8086e1ed7758460-1080.webp)

Begin at Goko-no-miya Shrine at 10:00 am for 40 minutes. This local shrine in Fushimi is a quiet place to start the day. Take a slow walk through the grounds, then pause at the main gate to look at its painted carvings. The grounds are free to visit. Find it at 174 Goko-no-miya Monzen-cho, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto.

At 1:30 pm, spend 35 minutes at Terada-ya, a historic inn associated with Sakamoto Ryoma. Tour the rooms and take a moment to notice how compact the building is. Admission costs a fee. The inn is at 263 Minamihamachou, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto.

Continue to Fushimi Sake District at 2:30 pm for 75 minutes. Stroll along the canal past the brewery buildings, and stop for a small sake tasting if you feel like it. Walking is free; tasting costs extra. The district is in Fushimi-ku, Kyoto.

## Day 2: Nishijin Lanes and a Kita Bath

![Painted illustration for day 2 in Kyoto: Nishijin lanes and a bath in Kita](/media/trip-story/ce4a5a37aee3c0f6a411ec2528edae29e56bd0b78499d79646069ab7c7207de6-1080.webp)

Start this afternoon in Nishijin District at 1:30 pm, setting aside 60 minutes to wander the side streets of this traditional weaving district. Look for woven fabrics in shop windows as you go. It is free to walk around. The district is in Nishijin, Kamigyo-ku, Kyoto.

At 3:00 pm, take 45 minutes for Kyoto Traditional Sweets. Choose a traditional sweet at a shop in Nishijin, and ask which one they make for the season. The cost varies by order, and shops are in various locations across Kyoto.

Finish at Funaoka Onsen at 5:30 pm, with 60 minutes for a warm soak in this historic bathhouse. Look for the old tilework and carved wood inside; its interior is a lovely part of the visit. Bath admission costs a fee. The bathhouse is at 82-1 Murasakino Minamifunaokacho, Kita-ku, Kyoto.

## Plan your own trip

Start from this route and change any stop in the [Kyoto trip planner](/itineraries/new?city=Kyoto).

title: How to pay in Tokyo as a visitor: cards, cash, transit cards and ATMs
description: Plan how to pay in Tokyo with cards, yen cash, Welcome Suica, overseas wallets and ATMs, with practical tips for a first visit.
published: 2026-11-23
updated: 2026-11-23
photo: /media/spot/65063bf2-32ad-44e8-8de4-8918fe074755/c1b428f4b8f8574fee6b1d90f0e228901528c1bdfd7e073de74d9aeafbc0ef2c.webp
photoAlt: Shoppers in a narrow lane of food stalls at Tsukiji Outer Market, Tokyo
photoSize: 1600x1200
photoCredit: Aimaimyi · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
---
In Tokyo, pay by foreign Visa or Mastercard at many hotels, chains and larger restaurants, and use yen cash for small businesses and places that may not take cards. For getting around, choose a physical Welcome Suica or, if you have a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch, Welcome Suica Mobile; withdraw yen from a Seven Bank or Japan Post ATM when needed.

## Where can I pay by card?

Foreign Visa and Mastercard work widely at hotels, chains and larger restaurants. Amex also works at many larger businesses. When choosing where to eat or stay, these cards are a practical way to pay at larger businesses, but don’t assume every shop or restaurant accepts them.

Check UnionPay acceptance before ordering. Ask before you place your order so you can choose another payment method if needed. Many urban taxis accept cards, but a small restaurant or a business in a rural area may require cash. Keep yen available for those situations rather than relying on a card for every payment.

As of 2026-10, the general PIN bypass for card payments ended in March 2025. Know your card PIN before you travel. If a payment terminal requests it, signing may not replace entering your PIN, so check that you can use your card with a PIN before setting out.

For more payment guidance, see Localley’s [Japan payment tips](/help/japan/pay).

## How much yen cash should I carry?

Carry yen for markets, small restaurants, shrines, lockers and rural transport. These are the kinds of stops where cash may be needed, even if you use a card at larger businesses. Keep JPY1,000 notes and coins with you, so you have smaller amounts available for purchases.

As of 2026-10, a suggested daily cash reserve is JPY5,000–10,000 for casual meals, markets and small purchases. Carry more if you plan to shop. Treat the reserve as a practical starting point: your needs depend on what you plan to do, and the cash should cover the places where you cannot use your preferred card.

Before leaving for a day out, check that you have yen in smaller notes and coins. That way, a cash-only purchase or a stop at a small restaurant does not depend on finding a card terminal.

## Which Welcome Suica should I use?

You can buy a physical Welcome Suica at designated JR East airport machines. Reload that physical card with cash. If you want to use a physical card, remember that reloading it is a cash task; plan to have yen available.

Welcome Suica Mobile is another option for visitors with compatible iPhones and Apple Watches. It launched in March 2025 and supports Apple Pay card reloads. Check whether your device is compatible before choosing this option, and use Apple Pay to reload the mobile card.

As of 2026-10, Welcome Suica balances are non-refundable. Physical cards expire after 28 days, while Welcome Suica Mobile expires after 180 days. Keep those limits in mind when deciding how much to load, and avoid adding more than you expect to use.

## Where can I withdraw yen?

Seven Bank machines inside 7-Eleven accept major foreign networks, including Amex and UnionPay. Japan Post is another reliable option. These are places to consider when you need yen for cash-only purchases or want to replenish the cash you carry.

As of 2026-10, Japan Post charges JPY220, while Seven Bank fees depend on the card. Your card issuer may also charge a fee, so check its fees before withdrawing. At the ATM, choose yen, cover your PIN as you enter it and check the fee details shown before completing the withdrawal.

## Can I use a QR wallet, and should I tip?

If you already use a supported wallet, including Alipay or GCash, you can scan participating PayPay merchant codes with your home wallet. Support applies at participating merchants, so don’t assume every shop displaying a QR code will accept your wallet. Check that your wallet supports payments in Japan before departure.

As of 2026-10, PayPay expanded support to 35 overseas payment services in June 2026. The expanded support does not mean every wallet is supported. Check your home wallet’s Japan support before your trip, and have yen or a card available in case a merchant does not participate.

Tipping is not customary. Pay the bill, including any stated service or table charge. Check the bill for a stated charge and pay it as part of the amount due; there is no need to add a tip.

## FAQ

### Should I rely on my card for every purchase?

No. Cards work widely at hotels, chains and larger restaurants, but small restaurants and rural businesses may require cash. Carry yen for those stops, markets, shrines, lockers and rural transport.

### Can I reload a physical Welcome Suica with a card?

The physical Welcome Suica is reloaded with cash. Welcome Suica Mobile supports Apple Pay card reloads for compatible iPhones and Apple Watches.

### Should I choose my home currency at an ATM?

Choose yen. Cover your PIN while entering it, and check both the ATM fee and your issuer’s fees before you withdraw.

### Should I leave a tip after a meal?

Tipping is not customary. Pay the bill, including any stated service or table charge.

### How can I plan payments around my itinerary?

Match your payment options to the places you plan to visit: carry yen for cash-needed stops, and check card or wallet acceptance before ordering. You can [plan a Tokyo itinerary](/itineraries/new?city=Tokyo) and consider where you may want cash on hand.

title: How to pay in Singapore as a visitor: cards, cash, transit cards and ATMs
description: Plan how to pay in Singapore with cards, cash, transit cards, QR wallets and ATMs, including practical tips for first-time visitors.
published: 2026-11-13
updated: 2026-11-20
photo: /media/spot/d402183b-98b8-4eca-af50-823eeabad221/538c6a69504502d9d057a22b75f0645cc84e45732eec2f3df88bf4319f0f4d89.webp
photoAlt: Clothing and gift stalls with price signs in Singapore dollars at Geylang Serai Market
photoSize: 1600x1200
photoCredit: Chainwit. · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
---
Foreign Visa and Mastercard work widely in Singapore shops and restaurants, while some stalls and taxis may still need cash. For buses and MRT, tap a foreign Visa or Mastercard, or use an EZ-Link card; as of 2026-10, foreign cards incur a daily transit fee, with an Amex exception described below.

Hawker centres are where cash and QR wallets matter most: before you go, browse [Localley's Singapore spot guide](/spots?city=singapore) or open a hawker page such as [Maxwell Food Centre](/spots/7cfbc9c5-d71a-48f6-aa40-c16bbd3ad763), [Lau Pa Sat Festival Market](/spots/8472321a-2ee7-47bb-b243-c85252fc96dd), [Tekka Centre](/spots/6b0b6946-31be-4d8e-b279-290c21974200) or [Tiong Bahru Market](/spots/95268f57-8d63-4cea-9e72-f3332b48df2e).

## Which cards can I use in shops and restaurants?

Use a foreign Visa or Mastercard as your first choice in shops and restaurants. They work widely, so you can usually pay by card for everyday purchases. Check with the merchant before ordering if you want to use Amex or UnionPay, since acceptance depends on the individual business.

For taxis, ask the driver whether cards are accepted and whether a surcharge applies before you leave. Many taxis accept cards, but acceptance and surcharges can vary. Keep cash as a backup in case your payment method is not accepted.

At hawker stalls, ask how to pay before you order. Some accept only cash or supported QR wallets, and seeing a card terminal at another stall or nearby business does not mean the stall you choose takes cards.

## How much cash should I carry?

Keep cash for hawker stalls, small purchases and taxi backup. A suggested reserve is SGD30–50 per day for hawker meals and modest market purchases. Carry SGD2, SGD5 and SGD10 notes; small notes make it easier to pay without running into change problems.

You do not need to rely on cash for every purchase. Use a card where it is accepted, then use your cash reserve for stalls or small transactions that need it. For more practical payment details, see Localley’s [Singapore payment guide](/help/singapore/pay).

## How do I pay for buses and MRT?

Tap a foreign Visa or Mastercard on buses and MRT. Supported phone wallets can also be used. As of 2026-10, foreign cards incur SGD0.60 per day. May 2025 brought transit access for foreign Amex cards and supported wallets without that administration fee.

Use the same card or device throughout your trip. That keeps your transit payments together under one payment method. If you start tapping your physical card, for example, keep using that card rather than switching to its phone wallet.

You can also buy an EZ-Link card at station service points and reload it with cash. Ticket offices refund eligible remaining value. Check whether the remaining value is eligible before you count on a refund.

## Can I use a QR wallet at hawker stalls?

Supported Alipay+ home wallets can pay participating merchants, including some hawker stalls. As of 2026-10, coverage included 25 overseas apps. Use an existing eligible wallet and look for its logo on the SGQR code before paying.

A PayNow-only code does not guarantee that a visitor can pay with a tourist wallet. Check the displayed logos or ask the merchant before placing your order, and carry cash in case the wallet is not supported.

## Where can I withdraw cash, and what should I check?

Foreign cards are accepted at ATMs operated by DBS/POSB, UOB and OCBC. Operator fees vary from zero to about SGD8, and your card issuer may also charge a fee. As of 2026-10, check the fee shown on screen before you accept the withdrawal.

Choose SGD when the ATM asks which currency to use, and cover your PIN as you enter it. Use a bank-attached machine when possible. These steps help you see the local-currency amount and keep your PIN private.

## Should I tip?

Tipping is not expected in Singapore. Restaurants and hotels often include a service charge, so check the bill rather than treating a tip as a required part of payment.

Planning your stops around where you want to eat and shop? [Start a Singapore itinerary](/itineraries/new?city=Singapore) and keep your travel plans together.

## FAQ

### Can I pay everywhere with a foreign Visa or Mastercard?

They work widely in shops and restaurants, but some hawker stalls accept only cash or supported QR wallets. Ask at the stall before ordering.

### Do I need cash for taxis?

Many taxis accept cards, sometimes with surcharges. Confirm card acceptance and any surcharge with the driver before departure, and keep cash as a backup.

### Does tapping a foreign card on transit cost extra?

Foreign Visa and Mastercard incur SGD0.60 per day. Foreign Amex cards and supported wallets gained transit access without that administration fee in May 2025; use the same card or device throughout.

### Can I use an ATM without paying a fee?

Operator fees vary from zero to about SGD8, and your card issuer may also charge a fee. Check the displayed fee before proceeding.

### Is tipping expected?

No. Tipping is not expected, and restaurants and hotels often include a service charge.

title: How to pay in Bangkok as a visitor: cards, cash, transit cards and ATMs
description: Plan how to pay around Bangkok with cards, baht cash, Rabbit and contactless transit, ATMs, tourist QR options and practical tips for first-time visitors.
published: 2026-11-09
updated: 2026-11-20
photo: /media/spot/c9f18f80-3b4d-4bb7-84b6-6972508be155/967676813ca12b0e4995808cdf605cbe9c164356ab8da0a854bbde9c33041401.webp
photoAlt: Flower and vegetable stalls along the street at Pak Khlong Talat, Bangkok
photoSize: 1600x1200
photoCredit: Sry85 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
---
For a first trip to Bangkok, use a foreign card at hotels, malls and larger restaurants, and carry baht for street stalls, markets and local transport. For transit, use Rabbit on the BTS, contactless bank cards on the MRT Blue and Purple lines, and a bank card on the Airport Rail Link; keep cash for the places and journeys where cards may not work.

Markets are where baht matters most: before you go, browse [Localley's Bangkok spot guide](/spots?city=bangkok) or open a market page such as [Chatuchak Weekend Market](/spots/a4f571b1-dafa-464e-8a20-927e2943eb9a), [Khlong Toei Fresh Market](/spots/a1197aa1-3563-45b9-8673-55ed1047d613), [Pratunam Market](/spots/e209dcec-c9cf-4bbc-a7bf-8470044279c3) or [Asiatique Night Market](/spots/93082bd7-4148-40a7-9b41-0047b520de38).

## Where can I pay by card?

Foreign Visa, Mastercard and UnionPay cards work at hotels, malls and larger restaurants. Carry a backup payment method, since street stalls and markets generally need cash. Tuk-tuks and most meter taxis also need cash, though ride-hailing apps can charge a registered foreign card.

Confirm Amex acceptance before relying on it. At smaller merchants, ask whether a card surcharge applies before paying. If a terminal offers to convert the amount into your home currency, choose THB instead.

For more trip-planning guidance, see Localley’s [Thailand payment guide](/help/thailand/pay).

## How much cash should I carry?

Carry baht for street food, markets, local transport and taxi tolls. A suggested daily reserve for street meals and modest market purchases is THB500–1,000. Keep THB20, THB50 and THB100 notes handy: drivers may struggle to change THB1,000.

You do not need to rely on large notes for small purchases. Before leaving your hotel or a larger shop, check that you have smaller notes available for fares and everyday spending.

## Which payment works on Bangkok transit?

For the BTS, buy a Rabbit card at a station office using your passport, then reload it with cash. Rabbit requires a physical card, and it does not cover the MRT Blue or Purple lines. Its purchase fee is non-refundable; ask a BTS office about a refund for eligible remaining value.

On the MRT Blue and Purple lines, you can tap a contactless Visa, Mastercard or UnionPay card. The Airport Rail Link added bank-card payments in November 2025. Keep baht available for other local transport and for journeys where your payment method is not accepted. As of 2026-10, these transit rules and payment options are current.

## Where should I withdraw cash, and what should I avoid?

Krungsri and SCB ATMs accept foreign cards. Use machines at banks or malls, cover the keypad while entering your PIN, and decline conversion to your home currency. Your card issuer may add its own fee.

As of 2026-10, Krungsri charges THB350 for Mastercard withdrawals; Visa and UnionPay withdrawals cost THB250. Check the ATM screen before confirming, and remember that an issuer may charge an additional fee.

## Can I pay by QR code?

TAGTHAi Easy Pay offers tourists QR payments through KBank PAY&TOUR. Register with your passport at a participating exchange booth. To fund PAY&TOUR, exchange cash at KBank and then link it in TAGTHAi. Do not assume that a foreign card can top it up.

Some supported home banking apps can pay participating Thai merchants through cross-border QR links. This depends on the app and merchant: ordinary personal PromptPay codes may fail. Keep baht or another accepted payment method ready if the QR payment is not available.

## Should I tip?

Tipping is optional. Rounding a taxi fare is common, and at restaurants you can check the bill for an included service charge before deciding whether to leave anything extra.

## FAQ

### Can I use a foreign card for every purchase?

No. Cards work at hotels, malls and larger restaurants, but street stalls, markets, tuk-tuks and most meter taxis need cash. Ride-hailing apps can charge a registered foreign card.

### Can I use Rabbit on the MRT?

No. Rabbit is for the BTS and excludes the MRT Blue and Purple lines. Those MRT lines accept contactless Visa, Mastercard and UnionPay.

### Should I accept an ATM’s conversion to my home currency?

No. Decline that conversion and use THB. Your issuer may still charge an additional fee.

### Can I add money to PAY&TOUR with my foreign card?

Do not assume so. Fund PAY&TOUR with cash exchanged at KBank, then link it in TAGTHAi.

### How can I plan payments around my itinerary?

Match your payment options to the places and transit you expect to use, and keep a cash reserve for street spending. You can [start a Bangkok itinerary](/itineraries/new?city=Bangkok) and plan where to carry cash or use a card.

title: How to pay in Seoul as a visitor: cards, cash, T-money and ATMs
description: What works at the counter in Seoul in 2026, which ATMs take foreign cards, how much cash to carry and the five Korean phrases for paying.
published: 2026-11-02
updated: 2026-11-20
photo: /media/spot/0d120515-c856-48cf-8621-7efad0e59568/8344c77eee82a6b933b39c70075c9bb9ca0f6784f27f6cdd95317d396ebdf64d.webp
photoAlt: Shoppers between the stalls of Namdaemun Market in Seoul, where many vendors still prefer cash
photoSize: 1280x853
photoCredit: Korea Tourism Organization / 니오타니 스튜디오 (KOGL Type 1)
---
Seoul is one of the easiest cities in Asia to pay in. A foreign Visa or Mastercard works in most shops, cafés, convenience stores and taxis. A few places still need cash, and the transit card is a separate step. This guide tells you what to carry, where cash still matters and what to say at the counter.

Cash matters most at markets: before you go, browse [Localley's Seoul spot guide](/spots?city=seoul) or open a market page such as [Mangwon Market](/spots/aee0ec5d-577b-4e3a-ab5e-d92c4b743202), [Songpa-dong Traditional Market](/spots/b95aa4bc-1f50-4ff1-a0e5-9c3dcc6a047d), [Jegi-dong Herbal Medicine Market](/spots/96bcfa8e-f46d-4fd8-b140-12db5d5678e8) or [Dongdaemun Design Plaza Night Market](/spots/60585537-cdae-491f-a518-6b75c231927e).

## Cards: your main way to pay

- Foreign **Visa and Mastercard** work widely in shops, restaurants, convenience stores and taxis.
- **Amex and UnionPay** work at many larger merchants. Ask before you order at small restaurants and independent shops.
- Most stores have **no card minimum**, so you can pay for one coffee or one bottle of water by card.
- Carry a **physical card**. Apple Pay and Google Pay with foreign cards work in fewer places than at home.

## Cash: keep a small reserve

You still need cash for traditional markets, street food stalls, small rural businesses and topping up a physical transit card.

- Carry **KRW 50,000–100,000** a day for food and market purchases.
- Ask for small notes: **KRW 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000**. Market stalls often cannot change a KRW 50,000 note.

## Transit: get a T-money card on day one

- Buy a **T-money** card at any convenience store (GS25, CU, 7-Eleven) or at participating subway stations.
- Top-ups on the physical card are **cash only** at most machines. Keep a few KRW 10,000 notes for this.
- Compatible Galaxy phones can use the **Korea Tour Card** app with reloads from a foreign card. Check your phone model before you rely on it.
- Convenience stores refund small left-over balances when you leave. Refunds above KRW 50,000 need the T-money Town office near Seoul Station.

## ATMs: use the "Global ATM" machines

- Use **Hana, Shinhan or KB** machines marked *Global ATM* or *overseas cards*. Ordinary domestic machines often reject foreign cards.
- Expect an operator fee of **KRW 3,000–4,000**, plus what your own bank charges.
- When the screen asks, **choose KRW**, not your home currency. The conversion offered at the machine costs more.

## QR wallets

- Alipay, WeChat Pay and UnionPay QR users can pay at participating **ZeroPay** merchants. Look for the wallet logos at the counter.
- Since September 2025, Japanese **PayPay** users can pay in Korea too. Finish the identity check in Japan before you travel.

## Tipping

Tipping is not expected in restaurants, hotels or taxis. The price on the menu is the price you pay.

## Five phrases for the counter

Show these on your phone if the staff do not speak English. The Localley [Korea phrase cards](/help/korea#h-pay) show each one in large Korean text and work offline once the page is open.

| You want to say | Korean | Say it like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can I pay by card? | 카드로 결제할 수 있나요? | Kadeuro gyeoljehal su innayo? |
| My card is foreign. Does it work here? | 해외에서 발급받은 카드인데 여기서 사용할 수 있나요? | Haeoeeseo balgeupbadeun kadeuinde yeogiseo sayonghal su innayo? |
| Is it cash only? | 현금만 받으시나요? | Hyeongeumman badeusinayo? |
| Where is the nearest ATM? | 가장 가까운 현금인출기가 어디에 있나요? | Gajang gakkaun hyeongeuminchulgiga eodie innayo? |
| How much is it? | 얼마예요? | Eolmayeyo? |

## Your first-day checklist

1. Bring one Visa or Mastercard and one backup card.
2. Withdraw KRW 100,000 at a Global ATM at the airport or the first big station.
3. Buy a T-money card at a convenience store and top it up with KRW 10,000–20,000.
4. Save the [How to pay in Korea](/help/korea/pay) page on your phone for the details.

## Plan the rest of your trip

Payments are one small part of a good day in Seoul. [Build a free Seoul itinerary](/itineraries/new?city=Seoul) with local spots, opening hours and travel times between stops. Your first plan is free without an account. For more plans and saved trips, see [Localley Pro](/pricing) or [create a free account](/sign-up).
